about: Hallucinate: why AI makes things up, told through Mata v. Avianca (S.D.N.Y. 2023), where ChatGPT invented six court cases. Factory #3. Narration-led: the voice is recorded first and every visual beat is keyed to its word times.

lines.text: This court case doesn't exist. ChatGPT made it up.
It's called an AI hallucination. A lawyer filed it in federal court.
So why does AI make things up, and sound so sure?
New York, 2023. A lawyer asks ChatGPT for cases.
lines.say: New York, twenty twenty-three. A lawyer asks ChatGPT for cases.

lines.text: It gives him six, with judges and quotes. Not one exists.
He even asked it, is Varghese a real case?
lines.say: He even asked it, is Var-gheez a real case?

lines.text: It said yes. Then it said it had double-checked.
The judge called its legal analysis gibberish.
The lawyers were fined $5,000.
lines.say: The lawyers were fined five thousand dollars.

lines.text: Here's the thing. It wasn't lying. It was guessing.
Remember, a chatbot just guesses the next likely word, again and again.
To a guesser, a fake case looks just like a real one.
lines.say: To a guesser, a fake case, looks just like a real one.

lines.text: The guesser always has a next word. No "I don't know" button.
lines.say: The guesser always has a next word. No I-don't-know button.

lines.text: Unless it's trained to use one. Here's the catch.
AI gets graded like a multiple-choice test. Blank? Zero points.
A guess might be right. So models learn to guess.
The old SAT had a fix. Wrong answers cost a quarter point.
lines.say: The old S.A.T. had a fix. Wrong answers cost a quarter point.

lines.text: In OpenAI's tests, a model that rarely skipped got 75% wrong.
lines.say: In OpenAI's tests, a model that rarely skipped got seventy-five percent wrong.

lines.text: One that skips when it's unsure? Wrong on just 26%.
lines.say: One that skips when it's unsure? Wrong on just twenty-six percent.

lines.text: One tracker has now logged over 2,000 court cases like this.
lines.say: One tracker has now logged over two thousand court cases like this.

lines.text: It always has a next word. Even when the answer doesn't exist.
